claims.claim: If an ICD's shock function is left on, shocks in the last hours or days of life are common. In one study that read the devices after death, about 3 in 10 people had been shocked in their last 24 hours.
claims.supporting_passage: Kinch Westerdahl 2014, Abstract: "We prospectively analyzed intracardiac electrograms in 125 explanted ICDs." ... "Ventricular tachyarrhythmia occurred in 35% of the patients in the last hour of their lives; 24% had an arrhythmic storm, and 31% received shock treatment during the last 24 hours." | BHRS 2024, Abstract: "If the ICD shock therapy is not discontinued, there is an increased risk that, as a person reaches the last days of life, the ICD may deliver multiple, painful shocks that are distressing." | Pitcher 2016, body text (Scite citation statement): "One important reason (but not the only reason) for considering deactivation of ICDs and CRT-D devices is to try to spare these people from receiving multiple shocks from their device as they are dying. Such shocks are relatively common during the last few hours or days of life 9." | Goldstein 2004, Abstract: "Family members reported that 8 patients received a shock from their ICD in the minutes before death."
claims.location: Kinch Westerdahl: Abstract, Methods and Results. BHRS: Abstract. Pitcher: section 'consideration of deactivation of devices during life'. Goldstein: Abstract, Results.
claims.pico_timeframe: Kinch Westerdahl: 125 people with an ICD who died, one Stockholm centre; device memory read after explant; outcome shocks in last 24 h and arrhythmia in last hour; no comparator. Goldstein: next of kin of 100 US ICD recipients who died; relative-reported shocks in the minutes before death.
claims.safe_wording: When someone with an implanted defibrillator (ICD) is dying, the device can keep giving shocks. A Swedish hospital read the devices of 125 people after they had died: 31 in 100 had received a shock in their last 24 hours of life. UK guidance says leaving the shocks on risks several painful shocks in the last days.
claims.qualifications: One Swedish centre; most devices were fitted after a previous dangerous heart rhythm (secondary prevention), a group more likely to be shocked. The US relative-report study found a lower figure (8 of 100 shocked in the minutes before death). Do not generalise 31% to everyone with an ICD. State the study and population in the same sentence as the figure.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Figures vary by study, population and method: 31% (device read-out, Sweden) against 8% (relatives' report, US). Al Jaff 2026 notes that post-mortem device read-outs are not routine, so contemporary data are scarce.

claims.claim: A do-not-resuscitate decision does not switch off an ICD's shocks; in practice many people with such a decision still have the shocks active near death.
claims.supporting_passage: Kinch Westerdahl 2014, Abstract: "More than half of the patients (52%) had a do-not-resuscitate order, and 65% of them still had the ICD shock therapies activated 24 hours before death." ... "Devices remained active in more than half of the patients with a do-not-resuscitate order; almost one fourth of these patients received at least 1 shock in the last 24 hours of life." | Wan & Chakrabarti 2021, full text: "Deactivation is performed at the bedside by a qualified member of the pacemaker or arrhythmia team after discussion with the treating health care providers, and with the consent of the patient or designated decision maker." | Nakazawa 2020, Abstract: "Of 39 patients with DNAR orders, 27 (69%) did not undergo deactivation."
claims.location: Kinch Westerdahl: Abstract, Results and Conclusions. Nakazawa: Abstract, Results. CMAJ: section 'Deactivation of an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator is painless, noninvasive and reversible'.
claims.pico_timeframe: 125 deceased ICD recipients, Stockholm; 52% had a DNR order; device status 24 h before death.
claims.safe_wording: A do-not-resuscitate decision does not switch the shocks off. That needs a separate conversation and a reprogramming of the device by the heart rhythm team. In the Swedish study, about 2 in 3 people who had a do-not-resuscitate order still had their shocks switched on the day before they died.
claims.qualifications: The mechanism (a separate reprogramming step is needed) comes from the CMAJ practice summary; the frequency comes from one Swedish centre. 'About 2 in 3' = 65% of the 52% with a DNR order. The UK DNACPR form wording itself was not opened.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Consistent with a Japanese single-centre study of 51 people who died of heart failure with an ICD (Nakazawa 2020): 27 of 39 (69%) with a do-not-attempt-resuscitation order had not had the device deactivated. No conflicting evidence found.

claims.supporting_passage: Al Jaff 2026, Abstract: "Records of 1606 ICD or cardiac resynchronization therapy-defibrillator (CRT-D) patients (79% male; mean age 67 ± 10 years at implantation, 73 ± 10 at death) who died between 2006 and 2022 were reviewed." ... Full text, Results: "Of the 671 patients with anticipatory tachytherapy deactivation, 176 (26%) were deactivated more than one month before death, primarily at an outpatient clinic (= 74, 11%). claims.claim: Switching off the shocks needs no operation, is painless and reversible, leaves pacing working, and does not in itself cause death.
claims.supporting_passage: Wan & Chakrabarti 2021, full text: "Deactivation of an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator is painless, noninvasive and reversible" ... "Deactivation does not interfere with ongoing pacing function or cause immediate death, does not immediately affect symptoms, and can be reversed if goals of care change." | McEvedy 2018, Introduction (Scite full-text excerpt): "Deactivation of an ICD does not lead to immediate death but does prevent the delivery of defibrillation shocks which have the potential to resuscitate the patient if they experience a fatal heart rhythm at end of life.5,6 Planned deactivation of an ICD is a simple, non-invasive procedure that can be carried out by a technician.7 In an emergency situation, placing a strong magnet on the skin will suspend shock delivery without interfering with the device’s ability to function as a pacemaker.7"
claims.location: CMAJ: headings and paragraph 3 to 4. McEvedy: Introduction (background citing UK 2016 guidance).
claims.pico_timeframe: Technical and practice facts about ICD deactivation (Canada; UK guidance cited by an Australian and US survey).
claims.safe_wording: Switching off the shocks needs no operation. A member of the heart rhythm or pacemaker team reprograms the device from outside the body. It is painless and can be reversed. The device's pacing (the part that stops the heart going too slowly) keeps working. It does not cause death by itself. It means that a dangerous heart rhythm near the end of life will not be shocked.
claims.qualifications: Say 'shock function', not 'the device'. Pacing continues. Deactivation removes a possible life-saving shock, so avoid implying it has no effect on how death happens. The magnet method is an emergency, temporary measure.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found. The UK guidance (Pitcher 2016; BHRS 2024) says the same, but its practical sections were not readable here.

claims.qualifications: Synthesis of mixed-quality studies and focus-group views; the findings do not give a single rate. Do not state how often this happens as a number.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found; the UK scenario study (Moffat 2016) and UFTO evaluation (Fritz 2013) point the same way.

claims.claim: A time-limited trial is an agreed plan to use a treatment for a defined period, after which the person's response decides whether to continue, stop and focus on comfort, or extend.
claims.supporting_passage: ATS 2024, Key Conclusions: "The time-limited trial in critical care is operationally defined as a collaborative plan among clinicians and a patient and/or their surrogate decision maker(s) to use life-sustaining therapy for a defined duration, after which the patient’s response to therapy informs the decision to continue care directed toward recovery, transition to care focused exclusively on comfort, or extend the trial’s duration." | Vink 2018, Abstract: "A TLT is an agreement to initiate all necessary treatments or treatments with clearly delineated limitations for a certain period of time to gain a more realistic understanding of the patient's chances of a meaningful recovery or to ascertain the patient's wishes and values."
claims.location: ATS: Overview, Key Conclusions; Section 1. Vink: Abstract.
claims.pico_timeframe: Critical care; consensus definition (Delphi with 100 stakeholders).
claims.safe_wording: A time-limited trial is an agreed plan to give a treatment for a set time. At the end, how the person has responded guides the next step: carry on, stop and focus on comfort, or extend the trial.
claims.qualifications: The consensus definition is written for life-sustaining treatment in critical care. Applying it to other decisions in older people is reasonable but is extrapolation; the report notes the approach is also promoted in nephrology, neurology and surgery. Quill & Holloway 2011 (JAMA) has no abstract and was not opened; cite ATS 2024 instead.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: The plan should state the treatment, how long it will run, the clinical signs that will show improvement or deterioration, and what will happen at review; it is proposed to and agreed with the person or family.
claims.supporting_passage: ATS 2024, Introduction: "This approach has been described as an attempt or “trial” of life-sustaining therapy, with specific, agreed-on guidelines designed to help clinicians, patients, and surrogates evaluate whether the therapy is providing benefit to the patient. These guidelines typically include a boundary on how long the trial lasts and clinical criteria that help determine the patient’s response to the therapy. After the trial is over, patients (if able), surrogates, and clinicians use these criteria to consider whether to continue life-sustaining therapies or, instead, focus exclusively on comfort ()." | Section 1: "Our committee concluded that the time-limited trial approach is distinct from current “usual care” for patients with critical illness, largely because of strong consensus that the trial is explicitly proposed to the patient and/or surrogate(s) who can then endorse the structured plan." | Section 2: "we measured participants’ views on these respective roles for three major elements of a time-limited trial:) the clinical criteria of improvement and deterioration,) the duration, and) the acceptable degree of recovery or the clinical outcome after the time-limited trial." | Key Conclusions: "A time-limited trial is composed of 16 essential elements that follow four sequential phases: consider, plan, support, and reassess."
claims.location: ATS 2024 full text: Introduction; Section 1; Section 2; Key Conclusions.
claims.pico_timeframe: Critical care consensus, US-led, 2024.
claims.safe_wording: Expert consensus describes what separates a time-limited trial from 'let's see how it goes'. The plan is offered to the person or family, who can agree to it. It names the treatment, how long it will run, the signs that would show it is working or not, and what happens at the review.
claims.qualifications: The four-item list simplifies the ATS consensus, which has 16 elements in four phases (consider, plan, support, reassess). Present the four as core items, not the full standard. The consensus is flexible: trials can be extended and should not be binding.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The ATS report says there is little evidence on how best to conduct trials. Kruser 2024 found them often carried out incompletely in practice.

numbers.meaning: essential elements in the ATS consensus, across 4 phases

candidates.reason: All essential claims are supported. Shocks near death: Kinch Westerdahl 2014, 31% of 125 Swedish decedents shocked in the last 24 hours; the BHRS 2024 guideline and 2016 UK guidance agree. A do-not-resuscitate decision does not switch shocks off: 65% of those with a DNR order still had shocks active 24 hours before death. Discussions come late: Al Jaff 2026 (1,606 Dutch decedents) found 42% deactivated, and 33% of deactivations happened on the final day; Goldstein 2004 found 27 of 100. Deactivation is painless, non-surgical and reversible, leaves pacing working and does not itself cause death (CMAJ 2021). UK guidance says people should have the opportunity to discuss it (BHRS 2024), which updates the 2013 BHF document. Use one shock figure, with its population and method in the same sentence, and do not generalise it to all ICD recipients.

The argument is supported for DNACPR, not for intensive care. UK guidance is that a DNACPR decision applies only to CPR, but it is known here only through how the NIHR 2016 synthesis reports it; the BMA/RCUK/RCN text itself was not opened. The same synthesis found DNACPR widely conflated with 'do not provide active treatment'. Beach & Morrison 2002 is a US scenario survey of stated intentions. The UK nurse scenario RCT (Moffat 2016) showed less monitoring and escalation with a DNACPR form, no difference with a whole-plan form, and no change in comfort care. The one-hospital before-and-after UFTO study (Fritz 2013) found fewer harms. ReSPECT places the CPR recommendation in a broader plan, with 78% of hospital forms and 87% of primary care forms recording other treatment recommendations. The opening line about intensive care has no source. The CQC 2021 claim was not found and must be dropped.
candidates.revised_angle: Open with a DNACPR (or ReSPECT) decision, not intensive care: 'A DNACPR decision is about CPR. It is not a decision about anything else.' Explain that UK guidance limits it to CPR, and that studies show forms are still read as 'do less' (UK nurses in a randomised scenario study planned fewer checks and escalations, with comfort care unchanged). Describe Beach & Morrison only as a US scenario survey of what doctors said they would do. Show the fix: record the CPR decision inside a whole plan (ReSPECT) that lists what continues; one English hospital saw fewer harms after doing this, which is an association. Close with the ask for families: 'What will still be done?' Keep the two-column 'not recommended / continues' visual.

candidates.reason: Supported, with Quill & Holloway 2011 (no abstract, not opened) replaced by the ATS 2024 consensus definition, opened in full text. The ATS text supports a plan explicitly proposed to and agreed by the person or family, with a set duration, clinical criteria for response, and a decision at review (continue, move to comfort, or extend). The four-item checklist simplifies 16 consensus elements and should be presented as core items. Chang 2021 must be labelled as a US before-and-after quality-improvement study in 3 ICUs, not specific to older people (mean age 64). Its results: markers of improvement were named in 21% of family meetings before training and 88% after, median ICU stay fell from 8.7 to 7.4 days, ventilation from 86% to 73%, and hospital mortality was unchanged at 58%. Surrogate satisfaction and conflict did not change. Avoiding both premature withdrawal and open-ended treatment is the consensus rationale, not a measured result. Kruser 2024 found trials often implemented incompletely, and Piscitello 2025 found them documented in 1% of goals-of-care notes.

The guide's order is supported by published descriptions: understanding and information or decision preferences first, then prognosis at the level asked for, then goals, fears, trade-offs and family. The trial results are supported: no clear effect on the co-primary outcomes (evaluated in 64 patients), fewer patients with moderate to severe anxiety and depression as secondary outcomes (the depression effect was not sustained), and more, earlier and better-documented conversations. The trial was in US cancer outpatients, not older people. The angle's claim that asking first makes the discussion 'shorter' was not found, and 'brings misunderstandings out early' is design rationale. The guide was revised in 2025 to 2026, so paraphrase it; do not quote it.
